title: No compulsion
hook: let there be no compulsion in religion (Quran 2:256)
tomorrow: Guru Nanak went into a river and didn't come out. then what?

segments.voice: Yesterday, nations and tribes made different on purpose, and ranked only by conduct. To know one another.

Across a holiday table, one relative leans on another: just believe what I believe. That isn't really an argument anymore. Yesterday's question was whether anyone can be made to. The Quran answers in its second surah: "There is no compulsion in religion." And there's a story behind the line. A report from Ibn Abbas, in Abu Dawud's collection, says that before Islam, some women of Medina whose babies kept dying would vow that if a child lived, they'd raise it Jewish. Later, when the Jewish tribe of Banu Nadir was sent out of Medina, some of those children were among them, and their Muslim relatives said: we won't let our children go. Then the verse came.
screen: `JUST BELIEVE WHAT I BELIEVE.` → `NO COMPULSION IN RELIGION.` → `THE CHILDREN OF MEDINA.`

segments.voice: Here's the debate, and Muslim scholars have stood on both sides of it. The first reading: this is a rule for everyone. Belief lives in the heart, and the verse goes on to say that the right way has become clear from error. Forced faith isn't faith, so no one may be forced. Read this way, the Medina story is one case of a wide law. The second reading, recorded by early commentators such as al-Tabari: the verse was a ruling about particular people at a particular time, and other verses and rulings shaped how far it reached. Its best case is serious. Read a law with its occasion. A ruling given about certain children isn't automatically a ruling about everything. Al-Tabari sets out several of these views side by side, and they all start from the same verse. So the verse itself is plain: there is no compulsion in religion. What Muslims have argued about, carefully, is how far that line reaches. A detail to keep: this verse comes right after the Throne Verse, a passage on God's power and care.
screen: `READING ONE: A RULE FOR EVERYONE.` · `FORCED FAITH ISN'T FAITH.` · `READING TWO: A RULING WITH AN OCCASION.` · `BOTH START FROM ONE VERSE.` · then, large: `NO COMPULSION.`

segments.voice: Rest your hands on your knees, palms open and turned up. Bring to mind one person whose path is different from yours, and keep the hands open while you hold them there: no grip, no pull. Let the breath come and go on its own.
No compulsion: Quran 2:256, there is no compulsion in religion, and the long argument about its reach.
Something to hold: no compulsion, in either direction, for anyone. That's the Quran, seven of seven.

chat.says: theo's mom wants him at his niece's baptism. he says church was forced on him for years. thoughts?
options: No compulsion cuts both ways: no one forces his faith, he doesn't force hers. Going is his call.
No compulsion means he should refuse every church event from now on, even family ones.
That verse is only about Muslims, so it says nothing at all about Theo's family.
chat.meaning: Quran 2:256 says there is no compulsion in religion: forced faith isn't faith. Theo's choice and his mom's faith are each their own.

tie.story: When some Medina families wanted to keep their Jewish-raised children, the verse came: there is no compulsion in religion.
tie.friend: Theo can choose freely whether to go, and his mom's faith is hers; neither has to force the other.
tie.you: whose path could you leave open-handed this week?

Ibn Abbas.meaning: a cousin of the Prophet, remembered as an interpreter of the Quran

Medina.meaning: the city where the Prophet settled after leaving Mecca

Banu Nadir.meaning: a Jewish tribe of Medina in the Prophet's time

al-Tabari.meaning: an early Muslim commentator on the Quran and historian

Throne Verse.meaning: Ayat al-Kursi, Quran 2:255, on God's power and care

sources.quoted: There is no compulsion in religion.

sources.ref: Quran 2:256 (the right direction is henceforth distinct from error); 2:255 (the Throne Verse)

Sunan Abi Dawud 2682 (Ibn Abbas: women of the Ansar whose children did not survive vowed to raise a surviving child Jewish; when the Banu Nadir were expelled, some of these children were among them; the Ansar said they would not leave their children; then 2:256 was revealed)
al-Tabari, Jami al-Bayan, on Quran 2:256 (the readings: a general rule; a ruling about particular people; questions of abrogation)
